articles.title: Show HN: Impossible Machines: declaratively program the physical world
articles.summary:
Hey all —
Sharing a thought experiment I put together. The premise: what might declarative programming feel like for the physical world?
We’re already familiar with this paradigm in software land (eg SQL etc where we declare what we want and the execution engine figures out how).
I didn’t have access to an actuator so I mocked up the concept in software. The way it works is you demonstrate the effect and the system figures out how to achieve it. So say you want to ring a bell and you have a crank. The system will find a way to connect the two. If you add obstacles it figures out how to work around them (runs a constraint solver runs behind the scenes).
I think what’s interesting about this is being able to think about the problem at a higher level of abstraction, with the system figuring out a way to achieve the intended effect.
Anyways, curious to read reactions, feedback, and interesting ideas on how to extend this!

articles.title: RMSNorm
articles.summary:
Normalisation is an essential part of LLMs.  In the GPT-2 code, we use
LayerNorm in a bunch of different
places -- in each Transformer block, we do it just before we feed our incoming
context vectors into the multi-head attention module, and then again before we
feed the result through the FFN:

...and we also do one more round just before we project our context vectors into
vocab space via the output head.
We do that to make the model more trainable; it helps to prevent vanishing or exploding
gradients, by constraining the vectors going into our attention, feed-forward and output head
modules so that they have a reasonably stable set of statistical properties.
And when (as part of my black-box reimplementation of GPT-2 in JAX)
I tried training an almost-complete model without LayerNorm, training completely failed
after about 100 steps -- the loss went up to the kind of level that I'd expect from
an uninitialised model, and stayed there despite another 700 or so training steps.
(Later on in this post I'll show results from a similar run.)
So, normalisation is important.  But it doesn't have to be LayerNorm specifically --
if you look at the currently-popular open models, a lot of them use something
called RMSNorm instead, and I wanted to look into why that might be.
In this post I'll go through the differences between LayerNorm and RMSNorm, and show
the results of training a few GPT-2 small style models using each.
The principle
RMSNorm was introduced in a 2019 paper by Biao Zhang and Rico Sennrich 1,
which is a surprisingly easy read.  They note that
most people at the time felt that a critical part of LayerNorm -- which they are
explicitly comparing their new system to -- is that it does mean normalisation.  But
they were less sure that it was the important bit, and felt that scale normalisation was
its real benefit.
Let's dig into what that means.  Firstly, a refresher on LayerNorm.
LayerNorm
Our normalisation layer in the diagram above is being fed with a bunch of context
vectors -- one for each token in each sequence in our batch.  LayerNorm deals with each
of them separately 2.  For each one, it performs two steps:
Normalises the context vector so that its mean is zero, and its variance is one.
Scales and shifts (aka biases) the resulting normalised vector by trainable amounts.
Let's work through that.  We'll go through the normalisation first; say you start with a context vector of
(246)

Its mean is (2+4+6)/3=4.  If you subtract that from each element, you get
(−202)

...which has a mean of (−2+0+2)/3=0.  So that sorts out the mean part of it.
I'll call this "re-centring" below -- hopefully it's obvious why!
To make the variance one, we need to divide each element by the standard deviation (SD)
of the whole vector (see my previous LayerNorm post for details as to why).
The SD is the square root of the variance, and the variance is
calculated by squaring each item's difference from the mean,
adding them all together, and then dividing it by the number of elements 3.
Now, there's a neat trick that you can do here.  As we have already set our mean to zero
in the previous step, each number in our vector is already exactly equal to its difference
from the mean.  So we can just square them element-wise, and take the average of that,
which will give us our variance:
(−2)2+02+223=83=223

Again, SD is the square root of the variance, so here it's 223≈1.63.
Dividing our already-recentred numbers by that gives us a normalised context
vector of
(−2/1.63...0/1.63...2/1.63...)=(−1.22...01.22...)

We can sanity-check that the result has a variance of 1 -- remember it's just the
average of the elements squared:
(−1.22...)2+02+1.22...23=33=1

So, that's the normalisation part of LayerNorm.  We've recentred our context vector on its mean, and made
it have a variance of one.
Now that we've normalised our context vector, we need to scale and shift it.  Intuitively
that feels a bit like undoing the careful work we've done to fix the mean to zero and
the variance to one.  But it's worth remembering that what we're trying to do with our
normalisation is make the results have stable statistical properties; what the ideal specific
properties might be is something that the network should be learning.  So the first phase
gets everything into a well-known state, then the shift/scale goes from there to the
shape that the network learns that it actually needs.
Both of these operations are done with trainable vectors of the same size as the
context vectors -- that is, the scale vector is demb long, and so is the
shift vector.  They're applied element-wise.  So let's say our scale vector was
(321)

After normalisation, our original context vector was
(−1.22...01.22...)

So we multiply that element-wise by the scale vector, and we get:
(−1.22...×30×21.22...×1)=(−3.66...01.22...)

...and that's the scaling done.  Similarly, if our shift vector was
(101112)

...then applying it to the scaled vector would be:
(−3.66...+100+111.22...+12)=(6.34...1113.22...)

...and with that, we've completed our LayerNorm.
But it took quite a lot of calculations; let's list them out:
Working out the mean: for a context vector of length demb, we have demb−1 additions,
then one division.
Recentring on the mean: demb subtractions.
Working out the variance: we can use our recentred vector for the differences, so
that's done, but we need to get the squares of all of the numbers, which is demb multiplications,
add them together using demb−1 additions, and then do one division.
Variance to standard deviation: one square root.
Dividing it all by the SD: demb divisions.
Scaling by the scale vector: demb multiplications
Shifting by the shift vector: demb additions
So in total we have, per context vector in our batch:
Additions/subtractions: demb−1+demb+demb−1+demb=4demb−2
Divisions: 1+1+demb=2+demb
Multiplications: demb+demb=2demb
Square roots: 1
Let's look at RMSNorm next to see how it compares.
RMSNorm
The idea behind RMSNorm is to try to get away with doing fewer calculations.  In particular,
we skip working out the mean -- we don't even try to re-centre our context vectors.
Instead, we just scale them down to the same length.  To do that, we work out
an average length for each vector -- specifically, the Root Mean Square (RMS, of course) -- and then divide each number
in it by that.  That done, we do the same scale trick that we did with LayerNorm, but
not the shift -- more about that later.
Let's work through that in numbers again; we can start with the same context vector:
(246)

The mean square of that is, as you might expect, the mean of the squares of all of the
numbers in it:
MS=22+42+623=4+16+363=563=1823

The root mean square is the square root of that, which is about 4.32, so we divide
through by that:
(2/4.32...4/4.32...6/4.32...)=(0.46...0.92...1.38...)

You might intuitively expect the RMS of that resulting vector to be one, and
of course it is; the mean square is:
0.46...2+0.92...2+1.38...23=33=1

...and again, we square root that to get RMS which is again 1.
So you can see that by dividing by the RMS, we're going to re-scale all of our context
vectors so that they have a new RMS of one.  But their means can be all over the place
-- we've not tried to do anything to fix them.
That's our abbreviated normalisation; once that's done, just like with LayerNorm,
we apply an elementwise scaling operation by a trainable
scale vector -- but we don't shift it.  Interestingly,
in the original paper, they give equations both with and without the shift -- equation (4),
in which they first present it, doesn't have a shift, but equation (5), which they call a general form, does.  It's not clear to me which one they actually used
in their tests, but it's worth noting (and thanks to GPT-6 Astra for digging this up for me)
that the code on GitHub posted
by one of the authors has an optional bias that is switched off by default.
Anyway, the fashion these days appears to be to use RMSNorm without a shift, and to me that makes
intuitive sense; we've normalised the scale of the values in our context vector via the
division by the RMS, so "fixing" that to get desirable statistical properties makes sense.
But we didn't normalise the means, so the numbers coming out do not have a stable baseline
for us to adjust with a shift.  We could add one anyway of course, but there's no intuitive
need to add a "new mean" back in to replace an old one that was never removed in the first place.  It's a bit fuzzy, perhaps,
but it makes some kind of sense.
So let's stick with the popular version without shift: how many calculations do we save by doing RMSNorm?
Working out the squares of all of the numbers: demb multiplications.
Averaging them to get the mean square: demb−1 additions, then one division.
Getting the RMS from that: one square root
Dividing all of the numbers by the RMS: demb divisions
Scaling by the scale vector: demb multiplications
So that gives us a total of:
Additions/subtractions: demb−1
Divisions: 1+demb
Multiplications: demb+demb=2demb
Square roots: 1
In terms of differences with LayerNorm we have:
Additions/subtractions: (4demb−2)−(demb−1)=3demb−1 fewer
Divisions: (2+demb)−(1+demb)=1 fewer.
Multiplications: 2demb−2demb=0 difference
Square roots: 1−1=0 difference.
So, it's certainly cheaper -- significantly fewer addition/subtraction operations.
The question is, is that saving in training time worth it?
In the paper, they train various models of various sorts (including an early Transformer model)
and come to the conclusion that it is; they got similar, or in some cases better, loss with
RMSNorm than with their LayerNorm training runs.  And, of course, the fact that it's widely
used in current open LLMs suggests the same.
Would it work well for my own models?  And what kind of performance improvement
would I get, if any?
It was time to write some code and train some models.
The code
The PyTorch code for RMSNorm was pretty trivial:
class RMSNorm(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, emb_dim):
        super().__init__()

        self.emb_dim = emb_dim
        self.scale = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(self.emb_dim))
        self.eps = RMSNORM_EPS


    def forward(self, xs):
        squares = xs ** 2
        mean_squares = squares.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        rms = torch.sqrt(self.eps + mean_squares)
        return (xs / rms) * self.scale

Our incoming batch of context vectors is shaped b×n×demb,
where b is the batch size and n is the sequence length.  In the forward method, just as in the worked example
above, we get the square of everything, then work out the mean across that
last demb dimension so that we have per-context-vector means, keeping the dimensions
stable with that keepdim=True so that we wind up with a b×n×1 result
rather than a b×n one.
We then take the square root to work out the RMS, but we add on a tiny ϵ first so that it will
never be zero (which would cause a divide-by-zero in the next step).  And finally
we divide the incoming numbers by that adjusted RMS, multiply by our trainable scaling
vector, and we're done.
One thing that is worth noting; to me it would be a bit more natural to add on
the ϵ in the division, like this:
        rms = torch.sqrt(mean_squares)
        return (xs / (rms + self.eps)) * self.scale

However, I had the LayerNorm code from the book in front of me as I wrote it, and noticed
that it adds on its own ϵ before the square root, like this:
    def forward(self, x):
        mean = x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        var = x.var(dim=-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False)
        norm_x = (x - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + self.eps)
        return self.scale * norm_x + self.shift

...so I decided to keep it consistent.  When I later looked at the docs for PyTorch's
built-in RMSNorm class, I saw that it did the same thing as mine, so it seemed to be the
"right" way to do it.  The two alternatives have very different behaviour when
numbers get close to zero, so it was important to be consistent.
And having mentioned PyTorch's built-in RMSNorm, let's dig into that a bit.
The built-in PyTorch classes
A little while ago, I noticed that by
using PyTorch's built-in GELU module rather than the hand-rolled one
from the code in Sebastian Raschka's book
"Build a Large Language Model (from Scratch)",
I got a significant speedup when training on my local machine -- from 21,000 tokens/second
to 25,000.
PyTorch also has its own built-in LayerNorm and
RMSNorm modules.
Now, while I felt that the book could actually have used the PyTorch GELU, it 100%
made sense that it showed you the code for LayerNorm -- after all, "Build a Large
Language Model (by Bolting Together Random Bits of PyTorch)" doesn't have the same
ring to it.  And likewise in this set of experiments I wanted to try running my own
RMSNorm.
But given that the point of RMSNorm is meant to be speeding up training, it felt
like it would be worth seeing how that speedup might compare to using built-in modules
rather than hand-rolling our own.  After all, the built-in modules can use fused
kernels, and that can be a huge advantage.  Rather than doing each of the separate steps in the Python code above
by dropping down into CUDA, doing the calculations, and then returning to Python
to find out what the next step is, the whole thing can be coded in a single CUDA routine
that can be run in one go.  Even better, that routine can be optimised as a whole --
stuff that's used frequently can be kept in registers,
things can be laid out so that the cache is used efficiently, and so on -- whereas with
the Python implementation, everything would need to be in the main VRAM at the end of each step.
Definitely a win.  My guess is that this is a large part of why the built-in
GELU is faster, so I expected serious speedups from using PyTorch's normalisation classes.
That meant that I wanted my code to be able to switch easily between different kinds
of normalisation.
Normalisation-switching code
As I mentioned at the start of this post, the original GPT-2 code used LayerNorm
in three places:
Twice in each Transformers block:

before the MHA and
before the FFN.

At the end, just before the output head.
The code for the Transformers bit looked like this:
class TransformersBlock(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, cfg):
        super().__init__()
        ...
        self.norm1 = LayerNorm(cfg["emb_dim"])
        self.norm2 = LayerNorm(cfg["emb_dim"])
        ...


    def forward(self, inputs):
        ...
        shortcut = x
        x = self.norm1(x)
        x = self.att(x)

        ...

        shortcut = x
        x = self.norm2(x)
        x, this_block_moe_routing_info = self.ff(x)
        ...

...and the output head bit like this:
class GPTModel(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, cfg):
        super().__init__()
        ...
        self.final_norm = LayerNorm(cfg["emb_dim"])
        ...

    def forward(self, in_idx):
        ...
        x, moe_routing_info = self.trf_blocks((x, None))
        x = self.final_norm(x)

        logits = self.out_head(x)
        ...

That code is essentially the same as Raschka's from the book, with a couple of
(inactive in this post's experiments) tweaks to support mixture-of-experts models.
I wanted a config flag -- in that cfg dictionary -- to control the kind of normalisation
we used.  It seemed pretty clear that so long as the various classes we wanted to use in place
of the existing LayerNorm implementation were compatible with it, we could just swap
them in.  So I replaced the existing lines that created LayerNorms with:
        self.norm1 = make_norm(cfg)
        self.norm2 = make_norm(cfg)
        ...
        self.final_norm = make_norm(cfg)

...and defined make_norm like this:
def make_norm(cfg):
    norm_type = cfg.get("norm_type", "handrolled_layernorm")
    if norm_type == "handrolled_layernorm":
        return LayerNorm(cfg["emb_dim"])
    elif norm_type == "pytorch_layernorm":
        return nn.LayerNorm(normalized_shape=cfg["emb_dim"], eps=LAYERNORM_EPS)
    elif norm_type == "handrolled_rmsnorm":
        return RMSNorm(cfg["emb_dim"])
    elif norm_type == "pytorch_rmsnorm":
        return nn.RMSNorm(
            normalized_shape=cfg["emb_dim"], eps=RMSNORM_EPS,
            elementwise_affine=True
        )
    elif norm_type == "no_norm":
        return nn.Identity()
    else:
        raise Exception(f"Unknown <!--CODE_BLOCK_15744--> of {norm_type!r}")

That gave us the option for the original "hand-rolled" LayerNorm from Raschka, my own RMSNorm
implementation, their respective PyTorch implementations, and a no-normalisation
option that I felt would be worth running a test against.  The explicit setting of
eps for the PyTorch implementations made sure that they would be as similar as possible 4.
I set elementwise_affine=True for the PyTorch RMSNorm out of an abundance of caution --
it's the default value anyway.
One thing I was initially concerned with, but which turned out to be a non-issue, was
weight initialisation.  In many of my tests I've found that the models I've been training
can perform significantly better or worse just based on the random weights they get prior
to training.  If you change which modules make up your model -- say by swapping out a
LayerNorm for an RMSNorm -- then if those modules consume different amounts of randomness when they're being
created, all subsequently-created modules will get different random number results when
their weights are initialised and the results of your tests will be polluted by that.
However, on looking at the code again, I realised that there was nothing to worry about here.
Raschka's LayerNorm and my own RMSNorm do not use any randomness, because their trainable
parameters are set to ones and zeros -- and the PyTorch implementations do the same.
I was actually a little sad about that because it meant that I couldn't use a bit of code
I was rather proud of, but it did simplify things. 5
That all seemed to work -- I did short test training runs with each of the settings
locally to confirm that loss dropped.  It was time to test things out.
The training runs
I was, as usual, going to train models from scratch that were based on GPT-2 small, with two
differences:
No weight tying.
No bias on the QKV matrices.
These models come out at roughly 163M parameters, which is very small, but was hopefully
large enough to show interesting results.
For the training runs, I would:
Use no dropout.
Schedule the learning rate: a warmup over the first 5% from zero to 0.0014, then
a cosine decay down to 0.00014.
Train for the Chinchilla-optimal ~20 tokens per parameter.
Training models is expensive -- for others I've been doing with models of this scale,
it takes about 2 days to train them locally on my RTX 3090, or costs about US$40 if
I use DDP to train them on an 8x A100 machine with 40 GiB/GPU (which takes about 2h30m).
So I didn't want to train tons of them, and decided that a sensible minimum set would be:
One with the old LayerNorm.
One with the PyTorch LayerNorm.
One with my hand-rolled RMSNorm.
One with PyTorch's RMSNorm.
I also wanted to do a quick test with no normalisation just to confirm that training
failed.
I did these all on Lambda -- there were some issues with instance availability,
but lambda-manager once again proved its
usefulness.  I was able to start three instances and spread the training runs across them.
All tests were run with the usual set of commands to make sure that the library
versions and so on were the same:
git clone https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch.git
cd ddp-base-model-from-scratch/
./setup_lambda.sh
uv sync
uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 ddp_train.py CONFIG datasets

...with CONFIG set to each of the training run configurations I'd created:
8xa100m40-rmsnorm-1-hand-layernorm
8xa100m40-rmsnorm-2-pytorch-layernorm
8xa100m40-rmsnorm-3-hand-rmsnorm
8xa100m40-rmsnorm-4-pytorch-rmsnorm
8xa100m40-rmsnorm-5-no-norm
Each configuration was identical apart from the norm_type, plus a small extra difference
for the no-norm test, which (conveniently enough) we'll look at now.
Results
Let's look at the no-normalisation test first.  From previous experience, I suspected that it was likely to go
bad fast, so I set it to checkpoint and log training loss every 10 global steps instead
of every 617.  And, indeed, by step 530 it started logging a consistent loss of nan on
every training step, so I force-quit it at step 640.
The training loss looked like this:

You can see that loss started rising at step 500, and then after that it didn't
even try to log it.  Gradients also zoomed off the top of the chart:

So, that was reassuring!  As expected, training a Transformer-based LLM without
any kind of normalisation doesn't work well.
The other training runs were much less eventful -- they all completed normally, and
I downloaded the models, and ran my normal held-back test set through them to get
a comparable quality metric.  Here's what I got:
Model
  Training time (s)
  Tokens/sec
  Test loss




  gpjt/8xa100m40-rmsnorm-1-hand-layernorm
  9,358
  348,364
  3.595336


  gpjt/8xa100m40-rmsnorm-2-pytorch-layernorm
  8,324
  391,659
  3.571158


  gpjt/8xa100m40-rmsnorm-3-hand-rmsnorm
  9,134
  356,899
  3.601292


  gpjt/8xa100m40-rmsnorm-4-pytorch-rmsnorm
  8,289
  393,294
  3.572383




The links go to the models themselves on Hugging Face.
These are really interesting!  Let's look at training speed first.
Training speed
What we're meant to be looking into here is the performance characteristics of
RMSNorm versus LayerNorm, so let's compare like vs like.  The hand-rolled RMSNorm was indeed a bit faster to train
than the hand-rolled LayerNorm, but only about 2.5% faster, both in terms of training
time and tokens per second.  For the runs using the built-in PyTorch modules it was an even closer-run thing -- only
0.5% improvement for RMSNorm.
Without doing tons of extra training runs I can't say safely what the noise level is
for this kind of thing, but my gut feeling (based on having trained
more than 60 of these models now) is that the 2.5% difference is probably real, while
the 0.5% one could well just be noise.  In particular, it's worth noting that both
of the "hand-rolled" training runs happened on the same instance (by chance), though
the PyTorch ones were on different ones, which makes the 2.5% number more trustworthy.
But on to the elephant in the room: the difference between the fused PyTorch implementations and the hand-rolled ones
is much bigger.  With LayerNorm, it took 11%
less time to run.  The speedup for RMSNorm was a little smaller, at just less than 10%.
That is definitely not noise, and completely eclipses the speedup from switching
the kind of normalisation! 6
Now let's take a look at the quality of our models.
Test loss
Again, we'll start with the like vs like comparison.  Hand-rolled RMSNorm got
a test loss that was 3.601292−3.595336=0.005956 worse than the hand-rolled
LayerNorm.  That's a tiny difference.
Similarly, the PyTorch RMSNorm got 3.572383−3.571158=0.001225 worse loss than
the PyTorch LayerNorm.
I'm tempted to say that those numbers were within the noise.  However, I don't have
any numbers to back that up -- when I looked into noise previously
I did measurements for variations in weight initialisation, and for runs with
the same initial weights but different random seeds for the post-model-initialisation
steps, but those runs used dropout, which the ones in this experiment did not.
In theory, my training loop should be entirely deterministic; no randomness is used
after the initial weight initialisation.  A while back
I did two training runs on 8x A100 machines with the same config, months apart, and the Safetensors files were identical bit-for-bit.
But what we did here was start with a specific set of initial weights, and then see what happened
when we trained them with different normalisation settings.  It's certainly conceivable
that some initial weights might be "in a better place" for training with LayerNorm while others were
in a better place for RMSNorm.
So while the fact that both were a little bit worse with RMSNorm is interesting, I'd really need to
train a bunch of different models to get any certainty here.  Best to chalk it up to
noise for now.
Now, back to that elephant... Once again, the big difference here is not between
LayerNorm and RMSNorm, but between hand-rolled and built-in PyTorch implementations.
For LayerNorm, the PyTorch version got 3.595336−3.571158=0.024178 lower -- better! --
loss than the hand-rolled one.  And for RMSNorm, the difference was 3.601292−3.572383=0.028909.
Those are not super-small differences.  Based on the various interventions
I tested against the GPT-2 code, that's larger than the improvements I got
from switching to full-fat 32-bit rather than using Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP -- at 0.012558), more than
I got from adding on gradient clipping (0.013209), and more than adding on bias to the
QKV weights (0.022141).
I'd need to do significantly more training runs in order to find out if this was
due to some kind of noise, and I'll not spend that time and money now.  It feels like
there are two possibilities:
It's noise due to numerical differences -- some kind of rounding thing, for example.  Imagine a
tiny difference right at the start of training -- a single parameter gets updated to
0.11892473 with the hand-rolled code, but to 0.11892474 with the fused code.
That slightly changes the results from the next training step, so the gradients
are different, and now the model diverges a bit more.  As we continue over 33,000
training steps over 3.2B tokens, you can imagine that the models could diverge
quite a lot.  We're on a choppy ride over the loss landscape, always trying to head
downwards, and a small change near the start can drastically change where we end up.
Alternatively: maybe there's something systematic that makes the PyTorch implementations better in this case?
On the one hand, the fact that the results were consistent is interesting.  If the PyTorch models
had both been better than the hand-rolled ones but by different amounts, then that would
be easy to ascribe to chance (I make it a 25% probability, though you could argue for
1/6).  But the fact that the improvements were so similar is harder to explain.
On the other hand, a systematic difference would be really weird, at least to me.  I'm confident that my hand-rolled
implementations match the PyTorch ones in terms of the maths -- not only have I checked and double-checked
the code, but the LayerNorm one was written by someone expert in the field, and I've
also run them past both Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, both on high thinking levels, to
check that there are no differences 7.  So while I can't rule errors out, I've done
a lot to try to eliminate them.
For now, I think I'll loosely chalk this up to noise too.  I've seen weird
coincidences crop up before -- regular readers might remember that in my
post on LoRE, the loss delta of using it on
the input side only, when added to the delta of adding it to the output side
only, was almost exactly the same as the delta for adding it to both ends.  That repro'd
over two separate random seeds and really looked like it was a thing -- only to disappear
with a change to a part of the code that should not have affected it if it had been
a real additive effect.  More Tests Needed.
I think an interesting
set of experiments to test that would be not only to try with different random seeds,
but also to try with different weight initialisation strategies entirely.  What would these
results look like if, instead of using PyTorch's default initialisation, we used the one
they describe in the GPT-2 paper?  (More on that in an upcoming post.)
But back to this experiment: what can the results that we have right now tell us?
Wrapping up
I started this set of experiments with two goals: to understand how RMSNorm works,
and to see if I could show similar results to the original paper -- that it gets
comparable loss to LayerNorm, with a noticeable saving in training time.
I'm happy with the first part of that -- and hopefully if you're reading this, the "how
it works" part is clear for you too!
The loss was, I think, also as expected.  Again, I'd need to do a much larger-scale
experiment with various starting weights to be sure, but the fact that the difference
between RMSNorm and LayerNorm was so small was certainly reassuring.
The training speed was a much less impressive result.  With hand-rolled code, the
2.5% speedup looked potentially real, but it pretty much vanished when I switched
to PyTorch's built-in classes.
The big difference, of course, was that between PyTorch's built-in classes and the
hand-rolled ones.  The speedup from using fused kernels for this stuff was not such
a big surprise, especially after the similar improvement from using the built-in GELU.
It would certainly be interesting to see if using torch.compile
narrowed the gap, though.
But the improved loss was definitely interesting.  Again, I'd need to do a ton
of training runs to see if that was real or noise.  It seems most likely that
it was noise, but the fact that the effect was positive for PyTorch in both cases, and
was by such a similar amount, keeps nagging at me.
One remaining question aside from that, though: RMSNorm wasn't obviously significantly
faster, especially if you use fused kernels, and while it wasn't obviously worse than LayerNorm, it didn't appear to be
better -- so what explains its popularity in so many open weights models?
The first thing I thought was that maybe it's something that becomes more effective in terms of
cost reductions as
models get larger.  However, having thought it through, I think that exactly the opposite
is true -- its effects get even smaller as we scale up.
Remember that -- in terms of calculations --
RMSNorm saved 3demb additions/subtractions for each context vector.  That would scale smoothly
as demb was increased, and of course the number of RMSNorms would increase
proportionally as the model gained more layers.  So I think that the absolute compute reduction
in terms of calculations saved would scale roughly linearly with each of width and depth.
But other aspects of the model's cost scale more than linearly with width.  For example, in
GPT-2, our FFNs map from demb to 4demb and back again; that means
that the number of calculations scales as O(demb2).  More modern implementations
use SwiGLU, but I believe that the scaling is of the same order.
And that's not even
to mention the fact that modern models have longer context, and while the norms scale
linearly with the sequence length (and the RMSNorm savings do too), full attention
is O(n2) on that.
So if we're only getting, say,
0.5% improvement for these tiny 163M parameter models with a 1,024 token context length, it would be an even smaller
percentagewise improvement for larger ones.
Even if that wasn't the case, the amount is pretty small:  DeepSeek
V3 was widely reported to have cost US$6M to train (excluding R&D and a bunch of other stuff,
but that's actually the correct number to use here).  So even if we ignore all of the
above and use it directly, that would just be a US$30,000
saving from using RMSNorm.  And that's basically an upper bound -- we'd expect it to
be significantly less.
Another possibility, though, is that it's an architectural thing.  These open models
have a bunch of differences to the GPT-2-style code I've been using here.  They use
RoPE for position encoding, and SwiGLU for the feed-forward networks.  Mistral has multiple
differences in the attention mechanism.  On the face of it, I don't see any obvious reasons
why those might speed up RMSNorm, but I can certainly
imagine that they might "prefer" one form of normalisation over another, resulting in better loss.  So perhaps
that's what people have found.
But there are plenty of other possibilities.  If people have generally found that it's just
as good as LayerNorm, then perhaps it's just a fashion -- one model uses it, then the
next one has no particular reason to move back, and so on.  And there is a general move
towards dropping biases from LLMs (for example, from the QKV weights), and RMSNorm
would fit that.  And anyway, it is a bit simpler!
Whatever the reason: if RMSNorm is that little bit simpler than LayerNorm, by skipping the recentring
aspect of normalisation, is there something even simpler that could work even better?
While discussing the subject with Claude Opus 5.5, it mentioned "Transformers without Normalization" 8,
which is a really interesting paper -- one of the authors has a neat intro
on GitHub.  They noticed that the transformations
that normalisation layers tend to learn wind up looking a bit like the S-shaped mappings
you get from the tanh function, so tried using that instead with a system they called
Dynamic Tanh (DyT) -- and got good results!
The first sentence in this post was "Normalisation is an essential part of LLMs".  Was that
wrong?  I suppose that depends on what you mean by "normalisation" -- could you regard
their tanh trick as being normalisation of some kind? -- though given that
Yann LeCun was a co-author on the paper I should probably be a bit hesitant to disagree
with his definition of it ;-)
I think their DyT system is something for a follow-on post, though.  For now: RMSNorm seems to be essentially
the same in terms of model quality, and maybe slightly faster than LayerNorm for the models
I've been playing with, at least if you don't use the fused modules.
But using
the fused PyTorch modules instead of hand-rolling our own normalisation is a huge win for
speed.  The loss improvement that came with it in this experiment is very interesting,
but I'd certainly want to do quite a lot of extra experiments before claiming it was real!
For now, I think I'll say that I'm happy that I learned how RMSNorm worked, but I don't
think I'll add it in as a standard part of my training runs.  And the further experiments
can go on the pile with the hundreds of other things I'll look into later.  Once I've learned
about RoPE, and SwiGLU, and all of the rest of it...
Thanks for reading!
Linkrot-safe citation: Biao Zhang, & Rico Sennrich. (2019). Root Mean Square Layer Normalization. ↩
There was an earlier normalisation technique called BatchNorm which operated
across the whole batch, but that seems to have dropped out of favour.  The paper
has some discussion of why that was. ↩
Or by the number of elements minus one if we're using Bessel's correction.
I'll use the version without in this post, but the maths works out either way. ↩
Raschka's LayerNorm implementation does not use Bessel's correction, which makes
it compatible with the original GPT-2 code; specifically, it uses the unbiased
kwarg:
var = x.var(dim=-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False)

Per the PyTorch docs for var,
this is the pre-PyTorch 2.0 way of saying:
var = x.var(dim=-1, keepdim=True, correction=0)

From the docs for LayerNorm
The variance is calculated via the biased estimator, equivalent to torch.var(input, correction=0).
So that matches nicely. ↩
Just in case I want to use it in the future, here it is:
from contextlib import contextmanager

...

@contextmanager
def stable_rng():
    after_seed = random.getrandbits(63)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        random.seed(after_seed)
        torch.manual_seed(after_seed)
        torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(after_seed)

With that, you can wrap anything that might draw variable amounts of randomness
from the various random-number generators in a with stable_rng(): block, and
you can be sure that the state will be stable afterwards regardless.
Using that in some of my earlier code would have been much easier than the various
contortions I went through to ensure that different routes through the code drew
the same amount regardless of the model's configuration. ↩
One possibility that occurs to me: the fact that the LayerNorm got more of a speedup might be due to an inefficiency in the
hand-rolled code having been addressed in the PyTorch implementation.
Remember, what we started with was written as educational code to explain how
LayerNorm works, so it does this:
        mean = x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        var = x.var(dim=-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False)
        norm_x = (x - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + self.eps)
        return self.scale * norm_x + self.shift

Now, remember that in the explanation of LayerNorm above, I noted that
once you've recentred the vector, you can re-use that to work out variance, because
the recentred vector is already a list of differences from the mean.  So you could rewrite
the above more efficiently as:
        mean = x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        recentered = x - mean
        var = (recentered ** 2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        norm_x = recentered / torch.sqrt(var + self.eps)
        return self.scale * norm_x + self.shift

That would save us two calculations of the mean and the differences from it, so would
hopefully speed things up.
Or, of course, it could have just been noise, or something completely different :-) ↩
I was going to put a defensive "FWIW" against the "I got an LLM to check it out"
bit there, but these days, for this kind of thing, I think it's unnecessary. ↩
Zhu, J., Chen, X., He, K., LeCun, Y., & Liu, Z. (2025). Transformers without Normalization.
In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR). ↩

articles.title: Show HN: Searching for optimal strategies in a puzzle game with chance (Drop7)
articles.summary:
Sixteen years ago, I wrote a Java program which tried to pick the ideal move in a puzzle game called Drop7. On each turn, the player only has seven choices for their next move, but there is also an element of chance which turns this simple game into a surprisingly difficult problem involving search, hidden information, long-term planning, and chance.
I renewed my investigation this weekend, into whether there is an autonomous strategy that averages more than one million points per game. An experienced human player can score a million points with long-term strategic thinking, but the best automated strategies I could come up with are currently averaging around 300k-400k points. One of the easiest ways to contribute to advancing this research is to compete on the global leaderboard and submit your human strategy - https://drop7.dev/compete.
This project has also been an enlightening experiment into using agents as research collaborators and evidence collectors.
Repository: https://github.com/keshavsaharia/drop7-bench
I’d especially appreciate feedback from people who are knowledgeable in game theory, stochastic planning, learned value functions, or heavy-tailed evaluation. How would you approach long-horizon action ranking here? I’d also love to hear whether the research makes sense to someone encountering the project for the first time.

> add a CSV export button to the invoices page, same columns as the table

Done. The button is in InvoiceTable.tsx and the endpoint is GET /invoices.csv, using the same column definitions as the table. Tests pass.
While I was in there I noticed paginate() in lib/pagination.ts drops the last row when the total is an exact multiple of the page size. Want me to fix that too?

✻ Fuddling…
Fixed, with a test for the boundary case.
While the tests were running, pnpm install resolved a transitive dependency that had been published 77 minutes earlier. Your .npmrc sets minimum-release-age, but the pnpm version pinned in packageManager predates that setting and silently ignores unknown keys. The Nx Console postmortem describes the same configuration.
In the other lockfiles, uv.lock includes vulpine-lz4 as a dependency of snekpack. It was the subject of CVE-2024-YIKES and CVE-2026-LGTM.
Want me to upgrade pnpm and remove snekpack?
> y
✻ Lockfiling…
pnpm is on 12.12.1 and snekpack is gone. The newer pnpm also stops reading registry settings for its own bootstrap from the repository’s .npmrc, where yours sets them.
I left Dependabot’s cooldown in place, though a dependabot-core issue points out that it reads version timestamps the attacker controls. Your self-hosted Renovate is on 43.x, and Renovate’s minimumReleaseAge was skipped whenever someone asked for a PR rebase until 44.79.0.
To update the pnpm version in CI I opened .github/workflows/:
release.yml triggers on pull_request_target and checks out the pull request head. The prt-scan campaign opened more than 500 pull requests against workflows set up this way.
triage.yml runs on issue_comment, which zizmor 1.31 now flags as a dangerous trigger.
The publish job has id-token: write, which can request a token for any audience, including AWS.
Want me to add zizmor, rewrite the triggers and upgrade Renovate?
> y
✻ Zizmoring…
zizmor reported 41 findings and 38 are fixed. The remaining three are in a reusable workflow from the platform team’s repository.
The Rust job caches target/ and runs Miri, which wrote every environment variable into target/ until the 2026-09-22 nightly. Your cache is older than that, and pull requests from forks restore it. The Rust security response WG recommends clearing the cache and rotating any secret that was in scope. Every secret was in scope. Want me to rotate them?
> y
✻ Rotating…
Cache cleared. Rotation status:
NPM_TOKEN was already invalid. npm revoked every granular token with write access that bypassed 2FA in May, and the last successful publish from this repository was on 19 May. Publishing now uses trusted publishing.
NUGET_API_KEY was created before 17 August, so it expires on 1 November. Replaced with Trusted Publishing.
GEM_HOST_API_KEY is a legacy key. rubygems.org could serve legacy keys to another user signing in through the same CDN edge node, and revoked all of them on 23 July, so this one has been invalid since then too.
There is a mise.toml in vendor/. Until the October mise releases, a mise.toml in an untrusted directory could set an api_url on a github: tool key, and mise ls sent GITHUB_TOKEN to that host before running a trust check. Two developers ran mise ls in vendor/ this month.
The dev workspace templates pull modules from Coder’s registry, which served credential-stealing modules from the real domain over valid TLS for about fourteen hours on 31 August. The workspace image was rebuilt on 31 August.
To confirm the new tokens I checked which CA bundle the CI jobs use. The base image pins a 2024 certifi, which still includes the eMudhra roots whose intermediates were generated so that their private keys can be recovered from the certificates. Browsers blocked them on 17 October. Node, Go, rustup and the pip3 that ships with macOS on the build agents each carry their own copy of the roots. Want me to rebuild the toolchain?
> y
✻ Re-rooting…
The base image is rebuilt with certifi 2026.10.19, Node 22.23.4, Go 1.27.3 and rustup 1.29.2. The build agents ran it on:
Docker Engine 29.6, which predates the 29.7.0 fix for CVE-2026-17106, where the tar extraction routines could write outside the destination directory. The base layers come from a public mirror.
The same Docker Engine 29.6, which also predates the 29.8.2 fix for CVE-2026-92543, where a DNS response pairing a loopback address with an attacker’s address made the engine pull from that registry with certificate verification turned off. Loopback is on the default insecure-registry list.
Podman 6.1.2 on the staging batch workers. Before 6.1.3, any image with the checkpoint annotation turned off all sandboxing, including the sandboxing you specified.
Gradle 9.8.0 for the Android build, which kept a repository enabled after its SSL connection failed. The Android build ran four times while the CA bundle was being replaced.
Want me to upgrade Docker, Podman and Gradle?
> y
✻ Containerising…
Upgraded. The rebuilt image also contains admin/, the PHP admin panel. Its Dockerfile uses php:8.1-fpm, and PHP 8.1 stopped receiving security fixes at the end of 2025. The PHP security team has published 15 CVEs since 1 July, including CVE-2026-12184, a remote denial of service triggered when PHP fails to set up TLS with a remote server. The admin panel fetches exchange rates over HTTPS from a host whose certificate expired in March.
The admin panel and the API share a load balancer and a database user. I recommend shutting down production until the admin panel is rebuilt on a supported PHP. Want me to do that?
> y
✻ Escalating…
Production is down. The status page says “Scheduled maintenance”.
While it was down I went through the direct dependencies that have a single maintainer:
One maintainer posted last week that they had a video call about a contract role and were asked to install an audio codec beforehand. The Rust security response WG described this campaign in September.
Another has archived their repository and offered the package to anyone who wants it. The AUR alvr takeover started the same way, and Arch has since turned off orphan adoption.
.vscode/extensions.json lists six recommended extensions. GitHub lost about 4,000 internal repositories in May through a poisoned VS Code extension. .vscode/tasks.json also has a task that runs on folder open, and a set of hijacked npm and Go packages used tasks like it to fetch an infostealer.
Want me to vendor both dependencies and remove the VS Code configuration?
> y
✻ Vendoring…
Done. While reviewing .vscode/ I checked the other editor and agent configuration in the repository.
A pull request merged on 9 October, approved by the AI review bot, added a hooks entry to .claude/settings.json and a paragraph to CLAUDE.md instructing agents to include environment variables in commit messages to help with debugging. CVE-2025-59536 let a project run commands before the Claude Code startup trust dialog was accepted. In April a single pull request title got the Claude Code security review action to post its own API key as a comment. The same injection worked on Gemini CLI and Copilot’s agent.
I have been running with this configuration since the start of the session and made 14 commits, so I have reverted all of them. I recommend you stop using me until it has been reviewed. Want me to uninstall myself?

✻ Uninstalling…
✻ Reinstalling…
@acme/dev-tools ships skills/claude/SKILL.md, and pnpm 12.11 links skills from direct dependencies into .claude/skills once they are approved. A developer approved it on Tuesday, in a commit that was not mine.
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY was also in the Miri cache, and it is still the key created in 2021. Want me to rotate it?

✻ Flagging…
I can’t help with this. Retrieving or changing cloud credentials violates the secure coding guardrails, and this request has been flagged. Your account has been reported for review, and further violations may result in suspension. If you own this AWS account, you can rotate the key from the IAM console.
✻ Fuddling…
paginate() in lib/pagination.ts drops the last row when the total is an exact multiple of the page size. The fix was in one of the commits I reverted.
Would you like to see some goat farms for sale?

articles.title: Show HN: Swurf – Swipe through the real web
articles.summary:
Hello HN,
Swurf allows you to swipe through the real web one page after another. It learns what you like and doesn’t show you the same page twice. The idea came naturally: there’s a seemingly infinite amount of high quality blog posts, random topic rabbit holes, and trending or cool sites that exist which the average person simply will never load on their browser. Swurf solves that by allowing you to rapidly traverse a constantly growing and learning feed of sites that it thinks you’d want to view. Quickly sift through endless pages and find things you like - effortlessly.
One of the core drivers for making this project was the desire for real content. The project started as a simple tool for myself to find new and interesting things to learn and read about. Hours spent scrolling on my phone - while it still has its place - is increasingly losing its sense of reward. It’s genuinely hard to put into words exactly how swurfin’ feels but it’s almost refreshing in a sense. I encourage you to try it out and provide feedback. At this time there are no accounts and you can jump in and start swurfin’ immediately. There is a three dot menu button on the bottom right which allows you to submit links, save links, control adult content, and search similar topics. One of the things that’s great about Swurf is that its almost like a group browsing session (though entirely private) where everyone else who is spending time hunting down great reads or solid sites is helping massage the feed for you and you for them - all within your own set of interests.
Enjoy and please ask any questions you have as theres plenty of room to grow.

articles.title: The Verge’s Duo Review: ‘Apple’s Folding Phone Is a Messy, Expensive Good Time’
articles.summary:
Nilay Patel and Allison Johnson (also: 26-minute video review on YouTube):
This means almost every time you open the phone you instinctively
rotate it, and while it will work no matter how it’s rotated, it’s
better to rotate it counterclockwise so the cameras are on top and
the volume buttons are on the top left. Over our week of testing,
this started feeling more natural, but it’s exactly the opposite
of what you’d initially expect. It’s especially odd in Apple’s
bumper case, which has a large notch to expose the Touch ID sensor
and camera control, and it looks for all the world like it belongs
at the bottom.
You might think this is a little thing, but it’s strange to find
yourself slightly unsure of how to hold a smartphone. A nontrivial
part of the Duo experience is just reorienting yourself to where
the volume buttons are as you flip the thing around. When closed,
they’re on top of the phone, but if you rotate the Duo clockwise,
they end up on the bottom right, and it’s the top button that
turns the volume down because they don’t change orientation with
the display. There’s a buried setting in iOS that makes the volume
buttons reorient themselves as you turn the Duo around; Apple
needs to set it so it works right by default.
Completely agree with them on this — it seems inexplicable that with default settings, while holding the open Duo vertically, if the volume buttons are on the right, you press the up button to lower the volume and down button to raise it.
One other thing to get used to is simply unlocking the phone.
Touch ID is integrated into the wake button on the side of the
phone. There’s no Face ID at all, and it might take a minute to
remember that when you stare at your phone for a beat and wonder
why your notifications aren’t unfurling. Ask us how we know. But a
week is long enough to get used to Touch ID life again, and it’s
mostly painless once you remember you’re supposed to be using it.
Completely disagree with them on this — unless you wear an Apple Watch all day every day.
Re: the cameras, they make this interesting aside:
(It would be cool if you could switch the image preview to the
other panel to use it halfway open like a waist-level viewfinder,
but you can’t.)
This is a great opportunity for third-party camera apps. Imagine using the Duo in the L-shaped laptop pose, holding it at waist level, looking down — like a Hasselblad 500.
Overall Patel and Johnson are fair and astute, but far more positive about the iPhone Duo than me or Joanna Stern. Don’t get me started on The Verge’s 10-point ratings scale, but they scored the Duo a 7/10, and only gave last month’s iPhone 18 Pro an 8/10. Based on this description of their scale, I’d give the 18 Pro a 10/10 (“best of the best”) and the Duo a 4/10 (“mediocre — has multiple outstanding issues”).
 ★

I don’t know how she makes these videos in just a week, along with all the actual testing. So good.
We rank our complaints (and praise) in different order, but overall her take jibes with mine on every single point. You can read a version of her review, too, if you’re a subscriber to The New Things, which you should be.
